title: Public Engagement, By the Numbers: Where the Money Actually Goes
subtitle: Hong Kong’s public engagement effort is bigger than most people inside it realise. The Information Services Department’s 2026-27 budget is HK$651.1 million, and in 2025 the department assisted 680 public events across television, radio, digital, print, outdoor advertising and on-site activity. Election publicity alone carried a HK$177 million allocation. That volume explains something worth noticing: the formats are already built — the media plan, the roadshow, the roving exhibition, the souvenir. What increasingly separates a programme that lands from one that quietly does not is the last few metres: the sign standing where someone hesitates, the queue that explains itself, the form that is easy to complete. Everything upstream decides whether people hear about the event. Only the room decides whether they did anything. That is where we put our attention.

title: Strategic Nudges: Small Prompts, Measurable Behaviour
subtitle: The best nudge is not a louder message — it is a better-designed choice at the moment of decision. That one line separates two entirely different ways of changing behaviour. The loud way keeps adding pressure: more reminders, more urgency, more noise, all of it trying to change what people want. The designed way changes the decision itself — the form placed in their hand, the default already ticked, the sign standing exactly where they hesitate, the object given at the second it is needed. Nothing is demanded of anyone's willpower, and nothing has to be taken away from the experience. The right choice simply becomes easier to make than to avoid. Which is why the numbers on this page are not a story about persuasion. They are a story about design.
